q: Is Bihać safe for tourists?
a: Yes, Bihać is generally considered a safe town for tourists, and serious crime against foreigners is rare. The usual precautions apply: watch your wallet in crowds and do not leave valuables visible in your car. The biggest practical risks are traffic, the river and ticks, not crime.

q: Is it safe to walk around Bihać at night?
a: The centre of Bihać and the riverside promenades along the Una are generally safe in the evening and busy in summer. As in any town, avoid unlit and deserted areas late at night. If you are unsure about a particular area, ask your host. In summer the streets by the river and in the centre stay lively until late.

q: Are there landmines around Bihać?
a: Some remote forest and mountain areas of Una-Sana Canton still contain suspected minefields from the war of the 1990s. The town, villages, roads, established picnic areas and marked trails in Una National Park are not in those areas. On trips, stick to tarmac roads, tracks and marked trails.

q: What do landmine warning signs look like in Bosnia?
a: Suspected minefields in Bosnia are usually marked with red triangular or square signs showing a skull and the word MINE. Sometimes they are also marked with tape or posts. If you see such a sign, do not enter the area and go back the way you came.

q: Is it safe to go hiking around Bihać because of landmines?
a: Hiking around Bihać is safe if you stick to marked hiking trails and paths that people use regularly. Do not wander into the woods, abandoned meadows or ruins, especially in remote and border areas. For longer routes, take a local guide or ask the local mountaineering club for advice.

q: How much of Bosnia is still mined?
a: According to the Bosnia and Herzegovina Mine Action Centre (BHMAC), in mid-2025 there were still just over 820 km² of suspected hazardous area in the country, about 1.6 % of its territory. Demining is ongoing, but no deadline for full clearance has been set. BHMAC publishes current maps and data.

q: What should I do if I see a landmine sign?
a: Stop immediately and go no further. Retrace your steps exactly, in your own footprints, and do not touch anything suspicious on the ground. If you are in danger or see an unknown object, call the police on 122. Never try to remove or move anything that looks like a mine or grenade yourself.

q: Are the trails in Una National Park safe?
a: Yes, the established, marked trails and viewpoints in Una National Park are intended for visitors and are used regularly. Danger only arises if you leave the trails and head through unknown woods or meadows. Follow the park's signs, and check information on the trails on the park's official website, npuna.com.

q: What is the police number in Bosnia and Herzegovina?
a: The police number in Bosnia and Herzegovina is 122. It works from mobiles and landlines, without an area code. For road accidents with injuries, also call the ambulance on 124. Call the police number for theft, road accidents or any threat to your safety as well.

q: What is the ambulance number in Bosnia?
a: The emergency ambulance number in Bosnia and Herzegovina is 124. The fire brigade is on 123 and the police on 122. Save these numbers in your phone before you travel, as they differ from those used in the EU. When you call, say where you are, what has happened and how many people are injured.

q: Does 112 work in Bosnia and Herzegovina?
a: The European emergency number 112 has not yet been introduced across the whole of Bosnia as it has in the EU, although work on it has been going on for years. On some networks a call to 112 may be redirected, but do not rely on it. In an emergency, call the police on 122, the fire brigade on 123 and the ambulance on 124.

q: What is the fire brigade number in Bosnia?
a: The fire brigade number in Bosnia and Herzegovina is 123. Call it for fires and also for some accidents that require rescue. In summer be careful with barbecues and open fires, especially in dry weather. If there is a wildfire, move away immediately and call 123.

q: Who do I call for roadside assistance in Bosnia?
a: Roadside assistance in Bosnia is provided by the motoring club BIHAMK; check its assistance number on its official website before you travel. If your car insurance or motoring club membership includes breakdown cover abroad, call them first. In an accident with injuries, call the police on 122.

q: Where is the hospital in Bihać?
a: Bihać has the Cantonal Hospital "Dr. Irfan Ljubijankić", the largest hospital in Una-Sana Canton, with an emergency department. In an emergency, call an ambulance on 124. For minor problems you can also go to the Dom zdravlja Bihać health centre. The hospital is a short drive from the town centre, but allow more time from more distant riverside villages such as Grmuša.

q: Is there a late-night pharmacy in Bihać?
a: Yes, there is always an on-duty pharmacy (apoteka) open in Bihać at night, at weekends and on public holidays, according to a rota. The rota is usually posted on pharmacy doors or published on local news websites. During the day several pharmacies are open in the town centre. Pharmacists often speak English and can advise on medicines for minor complaints.

q: Can I buy medicine without a prescription in Bihać?
a: You can buy medicines for pain, colds, allergies and stomach complaints at pharmacies without a prescription. Antibiotics and many other medicines require a doctor's prescription. Bring enough of any regular medication from home for your whole stay. If you need a prescription, go to a doctor at the Dom zdravlja Bihać health centre.

q: Is my European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) valid in Bosnia?
a: No, the European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) is not valid in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as Bosnia is not in the EU. Some countries have a bilateral agreement with Bosnia on emergency care, but you then need a special form from your health insurer. The safest option is to buy travel health insurance before you go.

q: Do I need travel insurance for Bosnia?
a: Yes, travel health insurance is strongly recommended for a stay in Bosnia. Without it you may have to pay for treatment yourself, as the European Health Insurance Card is not valid here. A policy is usually inexpensive and covers emergency care, hospital treatment and repatriation. Before buying, check that the policy explicitly covers Bosnia and Herzegovina.

q: Can Croatian citizens use public healthcare in Bosnia?
a: Croatia and Bosnia have a social security agreement, so insured persons may be entitled to emergency healthcare, but only with the certificate of entitlement to healthcare abroad issued by HZZO before travel. It covers emergency care only, possibly with a local co-payment. The European Health Insurance Card is not valid in Bosnia, so travel insurance is still a good choice.

q: Is tap water safe to drink in Bihać?
a: Yes, mains water in Bihać is generally safe to drink and residents drink it regularly. The town is supplied from the Klokot karst spring. In holiday houses not connected to the mains, with their own well or tank, ask the owner whether the water is drinkable. Bottled water is available in all shops and at petrol stations.

q: Can you drink water straight from the Una river?
a: Drinking water straight from the Una is not recommended, even though the river is very clear. It may contain bacteria from nature and from settlements upstream. For drinking, use mains water or bottled water. On trips, take enough water from home or from a shop.

q: Are there ticks around Bihać?
a: Yes, ticks are common in the grass, bushes and woods around Bihać and along the Una, especially from spring to autumn. Wear long clothing on trips, use tick repellent and check yourself after a walk. Remove a tick with tweezers as close to the skin as possible, slowly and without twisting.

q: What should I do if I get a tick bite in Bosnia?
a: Remove the tick as soon as possible with tweezers, gripping it right next to the skin and pulling steadily. Clean the spot and keep an eye on it for several weeks. If a spreading red ring, fever or joint pain appears, see a doctor and mention that you were bitten by a tick.

q: Are there venomous snakes around Bihać?
a: Yes, venomous snakes live in Bosnia, most commonly the nose-horned viper and the common adder, but bites to tourists are rare. Snakes usually hide in rocky, dry and sunny spots. On walks wear closed shoes, watch where you step and do not put your hands under rocks. Encounters with snakes while rafting or by the water are rare.

q: What should I do if a snake bites me in Bosnia?
a: Stay calm, keep still and immediately call an ambulance on 124 or go to the nearest hospital. Remove rings and watches from the bitten limb, and keep the limb still and below heart level. Do not cut the wound, suck out the venom or apply a tight tourniquet.

q: Is it safe to swim in the Una river?
a: Swimming in the Una is safe at calm spots, but the river has rapids, waterfalls and cold water. Do not swim near waterfalls and cascades, where currents and whirlpools can pull in even strong swimmers. Keep a constant eye on children, and do not jump in if you do not know how deep the water is.

q: Is rafting on the Una safe?
a: Rafting on the Una with a licensed operator is safe, with a helmet, life jacket and guide. The most important thing is to follow the guide's instructions and keep your gear on throughout. We organise rafting with Una Olympic Rafting from Grmuša, so get in touch on +387 61 591 320.

q: Can you swim under the waterfalls on the Una?
a: No, swimming under waterfalls and in rapids is dangerous because of strong currents, whirlpools and rocks. At Štrbački buk and other waterfalls the park's rules apply, so follow the signs. For swimming, choose calm, shallower spots with a gentle flow. Also watch out for slippery rocks and moss around the falls.

q: Is driving in Bosnia dangerous?
a: Roads in Bosnia are often narrow and winding, and some drivers drive faster and more aggressively than you may be used to. Drive carefully, keep to the speed limits and be ready for pedestrians and tractors in villages. From 1 November to 1 April winter equipment is compulsory in Bosnia.

q: Do I need vaccinations to travel to Bosnia?
a: No vaccinations are compulsory for travel to Bosnia. It is recommended that your routine vaccinations are up to date, and if you plan to spend a lot of time outdoors, ask your doctor about vaccination against tick-borne encephalitis. Discuss anything else with your doctor before you travel. Tick repellent is also useful for trips into nature.

q: Are there mosquitoes in Bihać?
a: In summer there are mosquitoes along the Una, especially at dusk and near still water. Bring mosquito repellent; windows in accommodation usually have screens. Mosquitoes here are generally not dangerous, just annoying. If you react strongly to bites, also bring an anti-itch gel.

q: Is Bihać safe for families with children?
a: Yes, Bihać is a quiet and safe town for families, with plenty of nature, parks and walks along the Una. The main thing to watch is the river, where children should never be left unsupervised. The riverside houses in Lohovo and Pritoka are pleasant for families, and you can send an enquiry on apartmanibihac.com.

q: Is it safe to leave my car parked in Bihać?
a: Generally yes, but as anywhere, do not leave bags, documents or electronics visible in the car. Park in well-lit, busy places or in your accommodation's car park. You can check whether your accommodation has parking in your enquiry on apartmanibihac.com. Lock the car overnight and do not leave the keys inside.

q: Where do I report a theft in Bihać?
a: Report a theft to the police on 122 or at the nearest police station in Bihać. You will need a police report for your insurance, so ask for one. If your passport or ID card was stolen, also contact your country's embassy or consulate. The police in Bihać sometimes have an officer who speaks English, but not always.

q: Is Bihać safe for women travelling alone?
a: Bihać is generally considered safe for women travelling alone as well. The usual precautions apply, as in any town, especially at night and in deserted areas. People are usually friendly and willing to help if you need information. Your host will be happy to recommend safe parts of town and places to go out.

q: Are there bears and wolves near Bihać?
a: Bears and wolves live in the mountain forests around Bihać, such as Plješevica and Grmeč, but encounters with people are rare. When hiking, walk in a group, talk fairly loudly and do not leave food in nature. If you see a bear, back away calmly and do not run.

q: Is it safe to swim in the Una after rain?
a: After heavy rain the Una can rise suddenly and become murkier and stronger, so swimming is not advisable then. Wait until the water level settles and the water is clear again. If you are unsure, ask locals or your host by the river. Murky, brown water is a clear sign that the river has risen.

q: Who can I contact for help at my accommodation in an emergency?
a: In an emergency, first call the emergency services: police 122, fire brigade 123, ambulance 124. For anything else, contact your host or us via WhatsApp and Viber on +387 61 591 320. We speak Bosnian, English and German, so we can also help you with translation.

q: Are there English or German-speaking doctors in Bihać?
a: Many doctors and pharmacists in Bihać speak English, and some also German, especially younger ones. However, this is not guaranteed, so it helps to have a translation app on your phone. If you need help communicating, contact us on +387 61 591 320. In an emergency, always call an ambulance on 124 first.

q: Is the summer sun strong in Bihać?
a: Yes, the summer sun in Bihać is strong, especially around midday, and reflection off the river and rocks makes it even stronger. Use high-factor sun cream, a hat and drink plenty of water. It is easy to get sunburnt while rafting because the water cools you down, so put sun cream on before you set off.
